title: A queue that wraps around

prereqs.why: This is the structure itself, and the indices-wrap-around trick is the whole idea.
You have just built a stack in an array; a queue in an array is the same exercise with two moving ends instead of one.
Every index is taken modulo the capacity, and getting that wrong writes outside the buffer.

statement:
Implement a **fixed-capacity FIFO queue** in an array, where the storage is
reused by wrapping the indices around. No `std::queue`, no `std::deque`, no
`list.pop(0)` - one allocation of `cap` slots, and both operations must be O(1).
In particular, **nothing may be shifted**: popping the front must not move the
remaining elements.

First line: `cap m`. Then `m` commands:

| Command | Print | When it cannot |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `push <x>` | `push ok` | `push full` |
| `pop` | `pop <value>` | `pop empty` |
| `front` | `front <value>` | `front empty` |
| `back` | `back <value>` | `back empty` |
| `state` | `state head <h> size <n>` | - |

`state` exposes the internals on purpose, so the wraparound is visible in the
output and a wrong implementation fails loudly rather than passing by accident.
`head` is the index of the front element - and when the queue is empty it is
whatever index the next pop *would* read, which is where the previous pops left
it.

```
input:   3 10            output:  push ok
         push 1                   push ok
         push 2                   push ok
         push 3                   state head 0 size 3
         state                    pop 1
         pop                      push ok
         push 4                   state head 1 size 3
         state                    front 2
         front                    back 4
         back
```

After three pushes and one pop, `head` is 1 and the next push lands at index
`(1 + 2) % 3 = 0` - the slot the popped element used to occupy. That is the
wraparound, and it is the only reason this structure is O(1).

### The point of the problem

A stack needs one index. A queue needs two ends, and the naive array version
makes one of them expensive: popping from the front of a plain array means
shifting every remaining element left, which is O(n) per pop and O(n^2) to drain
the queue. (That is exactly what Python's `list.pop(0)` does, and why `collections.deque`
exists.)

A ring buffer fixes it by **moving the head instead of the data**. The elements
stay exactly where they are; `head` advances, and when it passes the end of the
array it wraps to 0.

```
cap 4, after push a,b,c then pop:

index:   0     1     2     3
        [a]   [b]   [c]   [ ]        head=0 count=3
         ^head

after pop:
        [a]   [b]   [c]   [ ]        head=1 count=2     (a is still there, ignored)
               ^head

after push d, push e:
        [e]   [b]   [c]   [d]        head=1 count=4     (e wrapped into slot 0)
               ^head
```

### Two indices, or one index and a count

Storing `head` and `tail` is the obvious design and it has a famous flaw:
`head == tail` means both *empty* and *completely full*, and nothing in those
two indices can tell them apart. The classic fixes are to keep one slot
permanently unused (so full is `(tail + 1) % cap == head`) or to carry an extra
flag.

Storing `head` and `count` has no such ambiguity: empty is `count == 0`, full is
`count == cap`, and the tail is computed as `(head + count) % cap`. Use that.
The solution explains where the other design still shows up and why.

### Boundary cases

Pushing until full, then one more. Popping until empty, then one more. A full
queue that is drained completely and refilled, so `head` has wrapped at least
once. `cap = 1`. `cap = 0`, where every push is `full` and every pop is `empty` -
and note that a `% 0` anywhere in that case is a division by zero, so the
capacity check must come first. Interleaved pushes and pops that keep the queue
half full while `head` walks all the way round.

### Platform assumptions

`cap` is between 0 and 1000, `m` is at most 5000, values fit in a 32-bit `int`.
Indices are `std::size_t`, so `head + count` cannot overflow at these sizes.
Commands are always well formed.
hints: Keep `head` and `count`. The tail - the slot the next push should use - is `(head + count) % capacity`, computed when you need it rather than stored.
Pop reads `buf[head]`, then advances `head = (head + 1) % capacity`, then decrements `count`. The modulo is what makes `head` wrap from `capacity - 1` back to 0 instead of walking off the end.
Check `count == capacity` before computing any index on push, and `count == 0` before any index on pop. With `cap = 0` this also avoids `% 0`, which is undefined behaviour and in practice a SIGFPE.
